78.title: Anne and Joachim
78.hook: tradition names Mary's parents; their feast is kept on 26 July
78.howItsDone: Catholics keep the memorial of Saints Joachim and Anne on 26 July, pray to them as patrons of grandparents, and many churches and shrines, like Sainte-Anne-de-Beaupré in Quebec, are named for Anne.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Peter and Cornelius, and a door opened to every nation. Your line was no one is unclean to god. Who did you sit with? Day seventy-eight. A new week, and a whole week on one person: Mary.

Think of the person who taught you to tie your shoes. Who sat up with you when you had a fever. Who you don't think about much, because they were just always there. Every life has people like that, somewhere near the beginning. Mary did too. She had a mother and a father who carried her, fed her, and taught her to pray. And here's the honest part: the Bible never tells us their names. Not once. The Gospels open with Mary already a young woman. The names Catholics use come from a much older story, told outside the Bible. Today: Mary's parents.
screen: `WHO TAUGHT YOU TO TIE YOUR SHOES?` → `MARY HAD PARENTS TOO.` → `THE BIBLE NEVER NAMES THEM.`

segments.voice: The story comes from a second-century writing called the Protoevangelium of James. It's not in the Bible, and the Church has never treated it as Scripture, but its names and some of its scenes stuck. Here's how it tells it. Joachim is a good, generous man, but he and his wife Anne have no children, and at the temple he's shamed for it. So he goes out into the wilderness to fast and pray for forty days. At home, Anne sits in her garden and grieves. She looks up into a tree, sees a nest of baby birds, and weeps: even the birds have little ones. Then an angel comes to each of them, separately: you will have a child. Joachim hurries home, Anne runs to meet him at the city gate, and they embrace. Painters loved that moment for centuries. Their daughter is Mary, and Anne, the story says, dedicates her to God. Anne is the English form of the Hebrew Hannah, which means grace or favor, the same name as the mother of the prophet Samuel, who also prayed for a child for years. Joachim is usually explained as the Lord raises up. Catholics keep their feast together on July twenty-sixth, and since they're Jesus's grandparents, they're the patron saints of grandparents. Pope Francis even set aside a day in July for grandparents and older people, near their feast. The point isn't just a sweet story. It's that grace comes through ordinary families, slowly, through people who raised someone and are mostly forgotten.
screen: `AN OLD STORY, OUTSIDE THE BIBLE.` · `CHILDLESS, AND PRAYING.` · `THE EMBRACE AT THE GATE.` · `ANNE IS HANNAH: GRACE.` · then, large: `GRACE COMES THROUGH ORDINARY FAMILIES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank someone who raised you. Settle and breathe. Let a face come to mind: a parent, a grandparent, an aunt, a coach, a neighbor, anyone who helped raise you. Not the perfect version. The real one. Remember one specific thing they did: a meal, a ride, a word. Let yourself be grateful for that one thing. If they've died, you can hold them with love. If you pray, you can thank God for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Anne and Joachim. The names tradition gives Mary's mother and father, kept together on July twenty-sixth. Today's word.
Your line: someone raised her too. Today, tell the person you thought of, or someone who knew them, one thing you're grateful for. Day seventy-eight.

79.title: Conceived without sin
79.hook: Catholics teach that Mary was kept free of original sin from her first moment (defined 1854, CCC 491)
79.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the Immaculate Conception on 8 December, a holy day of obligation in many countries, and the United States has Mary under this title as its patroness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Anne and Joachim, Mary's parents in the old story. Your line was someone raised her too. Who did you thank? Day seventy-nine. Today, the moment Mary's own life began.

Here's a quiz a lot of people fail, including plenty of Catholics. What is the Immaculate Conception? Most people say: Jesus being conceived without a human father. Good guess. Wrong event. That's the virgin birth, a different teaching. The Immaculate Conception isn't about Jesus's conception at all. It's about Mary's. Her beginning, in her mother Anne's womb, conceived the ordinary way, by two parents. And about something the Church says was different about that ordinary beginning. On December eighth, 1854, Pope Pius the Ninth defined it as a teaching of the faith. Today: what it actually says.
screen: `A QUIZ MOST PEOPLE FAIL.` → `NOT JESUS'S CONCEPTION. MARY'S.` → `DECEMBER 8, 1854.`

segments.voice: Catholics believe every human being comes into the world carrying original sin, a wound from the beginning, a nature already tilted away from God. The Immaculate Conception says that Mary, from the very first moment of her existence, was kept free of it. Immaculate means without stain. And here's the careful part the Church insists on: this wasn't because Mary earned it, and it wasn't because she didn't need saving. The Catechism says it was a singular grace, given in view of what her son would do. A medieval friar named Duns Scotus explained it with a picture people still use. You can rescue someone by pulling them out of a pit after they fall. Or you can catch them before they fall in. Both are rescues. Mary, he said, was caught. Where does it come from? Catholics point to the angel's greeting, in the Douay-Rheims: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee." In Greek, full of grace is a single word that means something like one who has been, and remains, filled with grace. The Church reads it as a hint that grace was in her from the start, because God was preparing a mother for his son. Four years after the definition, at Lourdes, a poor French girl named Bernadette said the lady she saw told her, in the local dialect, I am the Immaculate Conception. Christians hold this differently. Orthodox Christians honor Mary as all-holy but don't define it this way, and most Protestants don't hold it. For Catholics it's a feast, December eighth, and a holy day.
screen: `IMMACULATE: WITHOUT STAIN.` · `KEPT FREE FROM THE FIRST MOMENT.` · `CAUGHT BEFORE THE FALL.` · `FULL OF GRACE, AND STILL FULL.` · then, large: `PREPARED FROM THE START.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for something prepared for you before you knew. Settle and breathe. Think back to something good in your life that someone set up before you arrived: a name picked out, a room painted, money saved, a door somebody held open years before you walked through it. Let yourself notice how much was ready for you. If you pray, you can say the angel's words slowly, once: Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee. The bell holds the time.
Immaculate Conception. Mary, kept free of original sin from her first moment, by grace, in view of her son. Not the virgin birth. Today's word.
Your line: prepared from the start. Today, prepare one thing ahead for someone else: a message, a meal, a clear path. Day seventy-nine.

80.title: Mother of God (Council of Ephesus, 431)
80.hook: the crowds in Ephesus cheered when the council called Mary God-bearer, a claim about who Jesus is
80.howItsDone: Catholics call Mary Mother of God in every Hail Mary and celebrate the Solemnity of Mary, Mother of God, on 1 January; Orthodox Christians call her Theotokos throughout their liturgy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Immaculate Conception: Mary's own beginning, kept free of original sin. Your line was prepared from the start. What did you prepare for someone? Day eighty.

Summer, in the year 431, in the city of Ephesus, on the coast of what's now Turkey. Around two hundred bishops have gathered in a church dedicated to Mary. The whole city is waiting outside. They've been arguing for months about one word, a word ordinary people used in their prayers. Late in the evening the decision comes out, and the crowd goes wild. People light torches and walk the bishops back to their lodgings, singing, with incense burning in the streets. All over one word. Imagine a city throwing a parade over a vocabulary question. Today's word is the word.
screen: `EPHESUS, 431.` → `TWO HUNDRED BISHOPS, ONE WORD.` → `TORCHES IN THE STREETS.`

segments.voice: Theotokos. Greek. Theos, God, and tokos, giving birth. God-bearer. Or, as it's usually put in English, Mother of God. Christians had been calling Mary this for a long time. But Nestorius, the archbishop of Constantinople, was uneasy. Surely, he said, Mary gave birth to the human Jesus, not to God. Better to call her Christ-bearer. It sounds careful. But Cyril, the bishop of Alexandria, saw where it led: to splitting Jesus into two, a man who was born and a God who was not. And the Church said no. Jesus isn't two people sharing a body. He's one person, truly God and truly human. So the one Mary carried and nursed and taught to walk is God the Son. Therefore she is truly the mother of God. That's why today's line is a claim about her son. Theotokos protects the truth about Jesus first. It doesn't mean Mary is older than God, or the source of God. It means the baby in her arms was God made man. Elizabeth said it first, in the Douay-Rheims: "And whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?" Catholics say the title every time they pray the Hail Mary: "Holy Mary, Mother of God, pray for us sinners, now and at the hour of our death. Amen." And the Church begins every new year with it: January first is the Solemnity of Mary, the Mother of God. Orthodox Christians use the Greek word in their prayers constantly.
screen: `THEOS AND TOKOS: GOD-BEARER.` · `NOT JUST CHRIST-BEARER.` · `ONE PERSON, GOD AND MAN.` · `JANUARY FIRST, EVERY YEAR.` · then, large: `THE MOTHER OF MY LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one Hail Mary, slowly. Settle and breathe. If you pray, say the Hail Mary once, so slowly that each phrase gets a breath of its own. When you reach Mother of God, stop for a moment and let it land: the one she held was God. Then finish, and sit in the quiet. If you don't pray, you can just hear the words in your mind and notice what they're claiming. Either way, no rush. The bell holds the time.
Theotokos. Greek for God-bearer: Mary, Mother of God, a title that is first of all a claim about who her son is. Today's word.
Your line: a claim about her son. Today, when you hear someone honored, notice what the honor says about the people around them. Day eighty.

81.title: Seven sorrows
81.hook: the prophecy, the flight, the loss, the road, the cross, the pietà, the tomb
81.carry: a sword shall pierce thy soul
81.howItsDone: Catholics keep the memorial of Our Lady of Sorrows on 15 September, and some pray the chaplet of the seven sorrows, meditating on each one with a short set of prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Theotokos, Mother of God, and torches in the streets of Ephesus. Your line was a claim about her son. Did you pray the Hail Mary slowly, or hear it? Day eighty-one.

Forty days after Jesus is born, Mary and Joseph carry him into the temple in Jerusalem. It's a happy, ordinary visit, the kind new parents made. An old man named Simeon, who has waited his whole life for this, takes the baby in his arms and blesses God. Then he turns to Mary and says something no new mother wants to hear. In the Douay-Rheims: "And thy own soul a sword shall pierce, that, out of many hearts, thoughts may be revealed." Imagine walking home with that. Catholics have spent centuries sitting with what that sword turned out to be. Today: the seven sorrows of Mary.
screen: `FORTY DAYS OLD, IN THE TEMPLE.` → `AN OLD MAN, SIMEON.` → `A SWORD SHALL PIERCE.`

segments.voice: Tradition counts seven. The first is that prophecy itself. The second, the flight into Egypt: fleeing at night with a newborn, refugees, because a king wants him dead. The third, losing him. Jesus is twelve, and on the way home from Jerusalem they realize he's not in the group. Three days of searching. When they find him in the temple, Mary says: "Son, why hast thou done so to us? behold thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." Every parent who has lost a child in a store for three minutes knows that voice. The fourth, meeting him on the road to the cross. The Gospels don't describe that moment. It comes from tradition and the Stations of the Cross. The fifth, standing at the cross. The sixth, holding his body when it's taken down. Artists call that the pietà, which means pity or devotion. Michelangelo carved the most famous one when he was in his early twenties, and it's the only work he is known to have signed. The seventh, the tomb: laying him in the rock and walking away. Five of the seven are Gospel scenes, though the Gospels don't say outright that Mary was at the tomb. Two come from centuries of prayer. A religious order called the Servants of Mary, founded in Florence in the 1200s, spread this devotion, and the Church keeps the feast of Our Lady of Sorrows on September fifteenth, the day after the feast of the Cross. Here's why Catholics love it. It says Mary's faith wasn't a shield against grief. She wasn't spared. She was pierced, seven times, and stayed.
screen: `THE PROPHECY, THE FLIGHT, THE LOSS.` · `THE ROAD, THE CROSS.` · `THE PIETÀ, THE TOMB.` · `FAITH ISN'T A SHIELD AGAINST GRIEF.` · then, large: `THY OWN SOUL A SWORD SHALL PIERCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold one sorrow gently. Settle and breathe. Let one sorrow of your own come to mind, big or small, old or new. Don't try to solve it or talk yourself out of it. Just hold it, the way you'd hold something fragile in both hands. Mary didn't make her sorrows go away. She kept them, and kept going. If you pray, you can hand this one to her, and ask her to hold it with you. The bell holds the time.
Seven sorrows. The prophecy, the flight, the loss, the road, the cross, the pietà, the tomb: Mary's grief, counted and kept. Today's word.
Your line: a sword shall pierce thy soul. Today, be gentle with someone who is grieving, even if the grief is old. Day eighty-one.

82.title: Taken up (Assumption, 15 August)
82.hook: defined in 1950, Catholics hold Mary was taken body and soul into heavenly glory (CCC 966)
82.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the Assumption on 15 August, a holy day of obligation in many countries, and Eastern Christians keep the same day as the Dormition of the Mother of God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seven sorrows, from Simeon's prophecy to the tomb. Your line was a sword shall pierce thy soul. Were you gentle with someone's grief? Day eighty-two. After the sorrows, the end of Mary's story.

In much of Europe, the middle of August is when everything closes. In Italy it's called Ferragosto: shops shut, cities empty, families head to the beach. In France, Spain, Poland and plenty of other places, August fifteenth is a public holiday. Most tourists have no idea why. Ferragosto's name goes back to the Roman emperor Augustus, but the day itself is a feast of Mary, one of the oldest. And the Bible never describes the event it celebrates. Scripture doesn't tell us how Mary's life on earth ended. Not a word. So where does the feast come from, and why did a pope in 1950 make it a formal teaching of the faith? Today's word is the name of the feast.
screen: `FERRAGOSTO: EVERYTHING CLOSES.` → `A FEAST OF MARY.` → `THE BIBLE IS SILENT.`

segments.voice: On November first, 1950, Pope Pius the Twelfth defined it: Mary, when the course of her earthly life was finished, was taken up body and soul into heavenly glory. Before he did, he wrote to bishops all over the world asking what their people believed. The answer was overwhelming. Christians had been celebrating this in some form for well over a thousand years. Notice the word. Jesus ascended: he went up by his own power. Mary was assumed, from the Latin for taken up. She didn't rise by herself. She was received. And notice what the definition leaves out. It doesn't say whether Mary died first. Most Catholics, and the long tradition, say she did. Eastern Christians call the same August feast the Dormition, the falling asleep of Mary. Catholics often point to a picture from the Book of Revelation, in the Douay-Rheims: "A woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars." But the Church is honest that the teaching rests on tradition and the Church's faith, not one verse. Here's why it matters, and it's not only about Mary. The Catechism calls it a share in her son's resurrection and a preview of ours. Catholics say in the Creed that they believe in the resurrection of the body. Not escape from the body. The body, raised. The Assumption says that what God did for Jesus, he's already begun doing for one of us. In that view, your body, with its knees and scars and tiredness, isn't a shell. Catholics say it's part of you, and it's meant for glory.
screen: `NOVEMBER 1, 1950.` · `ASCENDED VS. ASSUMED.` · `THE DORMITION: FALLING ASLEEP.` · `A PREVIEW OF OUR RESURRECTION.` · then, large: `TAKEN UP BODY AND SOUL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: treat your body with care. Settle and breathe. Start at your feet and slowly move your attention up: legs, back, shoulders, hands, face. Notice where you're tired or sore or tight. Don't judge any of it. Just thank each part for carrying you today. Let your shoulders drop. If you pray, you can thank God for your body, as it is. If you don't, just be kind to it for two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Assumption. From the Latin for taken up. Catholics hold Mary was taken body and soul into glory, a preview of the resurrection. Today's word.
Your line: the body matters. Today, do one kind thing for your body: water, a walk, sleep, a real meal. Day eighty-two.

83.title: Guadalupe, 1531
83.hook: Mary appears to Juan Diego near Mexico City and roses fill his cloak in December
83.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate Our Lady of Guadalupe on 12 December, when millions of pilgrims visit her basilica in Mexico City; Saint Juan Diego's day is 9 December.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Assumption: Mary taken up, body and soul. Your line was the body matters. What kind thing did you do for yours? Day eighty-three. And remember that woman clothed with the sun. You'll see her again today.

December, 1531. Ten years after the Spanish conquered the Aztec capital. The old world of the Mexica people has been shattered: by war, by disease, by strangers who don't speak their language. On a cold Saturday morning, a middle-aged Indigenous man named Juan Diego, baptized a few years before, is walking to Mass. He passes a hill called Tepeyac, just outside what's now Mexico City. And he hears singing, like birds, but more beautiful. Then a voice calls him by name, tenderly, the way you'd call a child. At the top of the hill stands a young woman, shining. Today's word is the name she's known by.
screen: `TEN YEARS AFTER THE CONQUEST.` → `A HILL CALLED TEPEYAC.` → `A VOICE CALLS HIS NAME.`

segments.voice: Here's the story as it was later written down in Nahuatl, Juan Diego's own language. The woman speaks to him in Nahuatl too. Not Spanish. She tells him she is the Virgin Mary, and asks him to go to the bishop and ask for a church to be built on that hill. The bishop, a Spanish friar, is kind but skeptical. Bring me a sign. Meanwhile Juan Diego's uncle falls deathly ill. So when he goes for a priest, Juan Diego takes the long way around the hill, trying to avoid her. He's embarrassed. He's failed. And she comes down and meets him on the other path anyway. In the story she says, more or less: don't be afraid. Am I not here, I who am your mother? Your uncle is well. She sends him to the frozen hilltop, where he finds roses blooming in December. He gathers them in his tilma, a rough cloak woven from plant fiber, and opens it before the bishop. The roses fall to the floor. And on the cloth is an image of her: brown-skinned, dressed like a noblewoman of his people, standing in front of the sun, with the moon under her feet. That cloak hangs today in the Basilica of Guadalupe, one of the most visited Catholic shrines in the world. Historians debate the early records, and the Church doesn't require anyone to believe in any apparition. But millions do, and Catholics honor her as patroness of the Americas. And Juan Diego was declared a saint in 2002.
screen: `SHE SPOKE IN NAHUATL.` · `THE LONG WAY AROUND THE HILL.` · `ROSES IN DECEMBER.` · `AN IMAGE ON THE TILMA.` · then, large: `AM I NOT HERE, I WHO AM YOUR MOTHER?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for the people of the Americas. Settle and breathe. Picture the map, from Alaska to the tip of Chile. Let faces come: a migrant on a long road, a grandmother in a village, a kid in a big city, a family you know. Hold them one by one. If you pray, you can ask Our Lady of Guadalupe to be near them, the way she was near a tired man who took the long way around. If you don't pray, simply wish them well. The bell holds the time.
Guadalupe. Mary as she appeared, the story says, to Juan Diego in 1531, speaking his own language, roses in his cloak. Today's word.
Your line: she spoke his language. Today, meet someone where they are, in words they understand, instead of making them come to you. Day eighty-three.

84.title: Why Catholics ask Mary
84.hook: asking Mary to pray for us, as we ask friends to, not worshiping her (CCC 971)
84.howItsDone: Catholics ask Mary and the saints to pray for them, most often in the Hail Mary's 'pray for us sinners', in litanies that answer each title with 'pray for us', and on saints' feast days.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Guadalupe: roses in December, and a mother who spoke Juan Diego's language. Your line was she spoke his language. Who did you meet where they were? Day eighty-four.

You text a friend: big interview tomorrow, pray for me? Or: my mom's surgery is at nine, keep her in your thoughts. People of every faith do this, and plenty of people with no faith at all. Nobody thinks you're worshiping your friend. You're asking someone who loves you to stand with you. Now, a question Catholics get asked a lot, sometimes kindly, sometimes not: why do you pray to Mary? Isn't that worship? Isn't God enough? It's a fair question, and there's a clear answer. Today's word is the answer.
screen: `PRAY FOR ME?` → `WHY DO CATHOLICS PRAY TO MARY?` → `A FAIR QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Intercession. From the Latin for stepping in between, going to someone on another's behalf. Christians have always asked each other to pray for them. The Letter of James says, in the Douay-Rheims: "pray one for another." Paul urges that intercessions be made for all people. Catholics believe that death doesn't end the family. The saints in heaven are still part of the Church, still alive in God, and they can still pray for us. The Creed calls it the communion of saints. So asking Mary is asking the person closest to Jesus to do what friends do. And the Church draws a hard line here. The Catechism says devotion to Mary is essentially different from the worship given to God alone. Worship belongs only to God. Mary is honored, the most of all the saints, but honored, not adored. And she isn't a second savior. Paul writes: "For there is one God, and one mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus." Catholics agree completely, and they say that everything Mary does, she does through her son and pointing to him. Remember the wedding at Cana? She notices the problem and tells Jesus, they have no wine. Then she tells the servants: "Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye." That's Catholic intercession in two lines: she brings the need to him, and sends people to him. Christians hold this differently. Orthodox Christians ask Mary's prayers too. Many Protestants prefer to pray to God directly and ask only living friends to pray. That's the Mary week: Anne and Joachim, the Immaculate Conception, Theotokos, the seven sorrows, the Assumption, Guadalupe, and intercession.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask, and be asked. Settle and breathe. Think of one thing you're carrying that you haven't asked anyone to help carry. Then think of one friend you trust. Picture yourself asking them: would you pray for me, or keep me in your thoughts? Notice if it's hard to ask. Then turn it around: who might want you to pray for them? If you pray, you can hold them before God now. The bell holds the time.
Intercession. Stepping in on someone else's behalf: asking friends, and for Catholics the saints and Mary, to pray for us. Today's word.
Your line: pray for us. Today, ask one friend to pray for you, or to keep you in mind, and tell them what for. Day eighty-four.
